passage:
"You're really not going to send me your answers?" Hemant said, leaning on Raghav's locker.
"It's the internal assessment. I can't."
"If you were a real friend, you would."
"That's not fair, Hemant."
"Everyone else does it for me. Are you trying to make me fail?"
Raghav felt his stomach turn. He wanted to help, but the word "friend" was being used like a lock. "I'll study with you tonight. Not share my answers."
"Then forget it. Don't talk to me."
Raghav took a breath. "I'm sorry you're upset. My answer's still no."
After school he told the class teacher what had happened, and the teacher thanked him for saying so.

qa.q: What did Hemant want from Raghav?
qa.a: Hemant wanted Raghav to send his answers for the internal assessment.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as Hemant used the word 'friend'?
qa.a: Raghav felt torn, wanting to help, but sensed that the word was being used to push him, which turned his stomach. The pressure came from the guilt in the words, not from a real request.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that worked?
qa.a: Raghav offered to study together, kept his no clear, and afterward told the class teacher.

qa.q: How might Hemant have felt about being refused?
qa.a: Hemant may have felt anxious about failing and frustrated, though that does not make the pressure acceptable; a real request would have left room to say no.

grounding: A young adult recognises a request carrying guilt and pressure, keeps a clear no, and tells a trusted person.

passage: I'm Omkar, and for a few months Hemant, who I was seeing, kept saying things like "If you trusted me, you'd share your location all day." At first it sounded sweet, like he cared. Then he sulked for hours when I said I'd rather not. He said, "You must have something to hide." I felt guilty and small, and once I gave in. My older sister noticed I was quiet and asked what was wrong. When I told her, she said when someone asks you for something, you are still allowed to refuse. I saw it clearly then. I stopped sharing, told Hemant kindly that I'd talk about it with a counsellor if he didn't accept my answer, and asked the college counsellor for advice.

qa.q: Who noticed that Omkar was quiet?
qa.a: Omkar's older sister noticed.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when Hemant said 'You must have something to hide'?
qa.a: Omkar felt guilty and small, and even gave in once. The words twisted a private choice into a sign of guilt.

qa.q: What steps did Omkar take for protection?
qa.a: Omkar talked to the sister, stopped sharing the location, was clear with Hemant, and asked the college counsellor for advice.

qa.q: How might Omkar's sister have felt hearing this?
qa.a: Omkar's sister probably felt concerned and glad Omkar told her, and her reminder that you are allowed to refuse helped.

grounding: A young adult learns to spot a request with pressure and guilt, and shares it with a trusted person.

passage:
Counsellor's note, student wellbeing centre, Tuesday.
Jagdish, second year, came in today. He said he was confused rather than upset. His girlfriend has been asking for his phone passcode. When he hesitated, she said, "If you loved me, you'd have nothing to hide." Last week, when he went to his cousin's wedding instead of seeing her, she said she'd "tell everyone what kind of person he really is." He kept saying, "Maybe I'm overreacting." I asked him how he felt when she said these things. He said, "Guilty. And kind of scared." We talked about the difference between a request and pressure: a request leaves room for no. He noticed that his answer never seemed allowed to be no. I gave him the number of our peer support line and suggested he talk to a trusted friend or family member too. He agreed to come back Friday. He said his older brother already knows.
— Rafiq

qa.q: When will Jagdish come back to see the counsellor?
qa.a: Friday.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel when his girlfriend said these things?
qa.a: He said he felt guilty and kind of scared, and he doubted himself, wondering if he was overreacting.

qa.q: What helped Jagdish see the pressure more clearly?
qa.a: Talking through the difference between a request and pressure, and noticing that his no never seemed allowed.

qa.q: What would change if Jagdish had kept it all to himself?
qa.a: He might have kept blaming himself and giving in; sharing it with the counsellor and his brother gives him support and a clearer view.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to spot requests that carry guilt and threats, and sharing unsafe pressure with trusted people.

passage:
Wednesday night.
Saurabh called while I was packing for the college field trip to Hampi. He said, "If you really loved me, you wouldn't go for four days." I laughed, thinking he was joking. He wasn't. He went quiet, then said, "Fine. Go. But don't expect me to be here when you're back." My stomach dropped.
I sat on the bed for a long time. This is the third time. Last month it was "If you cared, you'd skip your cousin's birthday." Each time I gave in, and each time it felt worse.
A real request would sound like, "I'll miss you, can we call each night?" This isn't that.
I called Didi. She listened without saying "I told you so." She said I can go on the trip and still care about Saurabh, and that if he keeps threatening to leave, that's his choice, not my fault. She's coming over tomorrow before I leave.
— Disha

qa.q: Where was the college field trip?
qa.a: To Hampi.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when Saurabh said not to expect him to be there?
qa.a: Disha felt shocked and hurt, stomach dropping, and also guilty, since Disha had given in before.

qa.q: What did Disha do that was wise?
qa.a: Disha noticed the pattern, compared it with what a real request sounds like, and called Didi, a trusted person, the same night.

qa.q: How did Didi respond when Disha called?
qa.a: Didi listened without blame, said Disha could go and still care about Saurabh, said his threats weren't Disha's fault, and planned to visit before the trip.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising a request loaded with guilt and threats and sharing it with a trusted person.

passage:
Ankita: can I ask you something about work
Gautam: always
Ankita: my senior asked me to stay till 10 again to finish his slides. I said I have class at 8 tomorrow
Ankita: he said "a real team player would stay. and if you don't, I'll tell the manager you're not serious"
Gautam: wait, that's a threat
Ankita: maybe I'm being dramatic
Gautam: no. a request would be "can you stay? totally ok if not." this one only has one allowed answer
Ankita: he does it every week
Gautam: have you told anyone?
Ankita: no. scared it'll get worse
Gautam: what about the HR lady you liked at induction? or your mentor?
Ankita: my mentor is nice. she said come anytime
Gautam: call her tonight, before you decide. want me to stay on the phone after?
Ankita: ok. calling her now

qa.q: What time did the senior ask Ankita to stay till?
qa.a: Till 10.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling about the senior's demand?
qa.a: Ankita felt scared it would get worse and unsure, even wondering about being dramatic, which shows how the threat made the pressure feel normal.

qa.q: What did Gautam suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Calling the mentor that night before deciding, because unsafe pressure should be shared with a trusted person who can help.

qa.q: How does Gautam see the senior's request?
qa.a: Gautam sees it as a threat, not a request, because it leaves only one allowed answer.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising a workplace request carrying guilt and threat and sharing it with a trusted mentor.

passage: The bus stand at Wardha was nearly empty when Lavanya read Asif's message again. "If you really loved me, you'd send me your phone password. Why hide things?" Last week it had been, "If you loved me, you'd skip your cousin's wedding and meet me." Each time she said no, he went silent for a day, then called her selfish. Lavanya thought of her friend Shabnam's message that morning: "Can you lend me your notes? Totally fine if you need them." That was a request. This felt like a test she was meant to fail. She didn't reply. On the bus home she called her older cousin, Pooja didi, and read the messages out. Pooja listened, then said, "Thank you for telling me. Saying no is allowed, and this pressure isn't your fault. Come over tonight. We'll talk it through, and I'll sit with you if you decide to reply." Lavanya turned the phone face-down on her lap and breathed out.

qa.q: What did Asif ask Lavanya to send?
qa.a: Her phone password.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel about Asif's messages compared with Shabnam's?
qa.a: Lavanya felt uneasy and pressured; Asif's message felt like a test she was meant to fail, while Shabnam's left room to say no.

qa.q: What was the wise step Lavanya took?
qa.a: Not replying under pressure and calling a trusted person, Pooja didi, who listened, said no is allowed and asked her over that night.

qa.q: How did Pooja didi see the situation?
qa.a: As pressure that was not Lavanya's fault, and something to face together, with an offer to sit beside her if she chose to reply.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult spotting a request that carries guilt and pressure, contrasting it with a real request, and sharing it with a trusted person.
